soil-found-060.q: In what order do igneous minerals weather, and why?
soil-found-060.a: Roughly in the order they formed, Bowen's reaction series, because the weakest cation–oxygen bonds go first.

soil-found-011.q: How is a soil colour written in Munsell notation?
soil-found-011.a: As hue, then value/chroma, as in a Cecil soil horizon recorded as red (10R 4/8) clay.

soil-form-137.q: At weathering rates of 20 m per million years, how long do deep regoliths take to form?
soil-form-137.a: Several million years, and longer still in cooler climates.

soil-form-112.q: How does alluvium differ from colluvium in sorting, and why?
soil-form-112.a: Running water lays down alluvium, so it is generally fine-grained and well sorted; colluvium moves without running water and is poorly sorted.

soil-form-096.q: How much richer in manganese is black rock varnish than the Earth's crust?
soil-form-096.a: It holds manganese 50 to 60 times more abundantly than the crust's 0.12%.

soil-form-027.q: Which test separates a duripan from petrocalcic horizons and fragipans?
soil-form-027.a: A duripan slakes in KOH but not in HCl.

soil-form-076.q: Why does modern soil classification fit paleosols poorly?
soil-form-076.a: Geology, life and the atmosphere changed greatly over the record, notably at the Great Oxidation Event 2.42 billion years ago; an alfisol, a forest soil, could not exist before trees.

soil-form-124.q: In biosorting, why do large stones end up at the base of the biomantle?
soil-form-124.a: Burrowers move only particles smaller than their burrows, so larger stones settle and form a stonelayer there.

soil-phys-052.q: Under Stokes' law, why does settling velocity vary so much with particle size?
soil-phys-052.a: The excess weight grows with R³ and the drag only with R, so settling velocity grows with R².

soil-phys-092.q: How does the dry bulk density of a mineral soil compare with the density of quartz?
soil-phys-092.a: Quartz is about 2.65 g/cm3, but a mineral soil's dry bulk density is normally about half that, between 1.0 and 1.6 g/cm3, because the more pore space a soil has, the lower its bulk density.

soil-phys-115.q: What do relative densities of 100% and 0% mean?
soil-phys-115.a: 100% means very dense sand or gravel; 0% means extremely loose, unstable soil.

soil-phys-123.q: Why is a soil's bulk density always less than its particle density?
soil-phys-123.a: Bulk density includes the pores; particle density, typically 2.60 to 2.75 g/cm3, does not.

soil-water-153.q: Why do clay soils hold more water than sandy soils?
soil-water-153.a: Water clings more tightly to fine clay particles than to coarse sand grains, so clays hold more water while sands let it pass more easily.

soil-water-223.q: Why does a capacitance probe's reading depend mostly on soil water?
soil-water-223.a: Water's dielectric constant (80) is far above that of mineral soil (4), organic matter (4) and air (1).

soil-water-200.q: How quickly do plants recover from water stress after rewatering?
soil-water-200.a: Mildly stressed plants recover in 1–2 days, but after severe stress they regain only 40-60% of maximum photosynthesis the day after rewatering.

soil-water-208.q: How much can development cut infiltration?
soil-water-208.a: Felton and Lull (1963) found a potential 80 percent cut, and Taylor (1982) found construction cut infiltration rates by more than 77 percent.

soil-phys-218.q: At what suction is field capacity conventionally defined?
soil-phys-218.a: At −33 kPa (−0.33 bar), or −10 kPa for sandy soils.

soil-phys-206.q: What sets the wet and dry ends of the least limiting water range?
soil-phys-206.a: The wet end is the lower of field capacity and the water content leaving 10% air-filled porosity; the dry end is the higher of the permanent wilting point and the water content at which penetration resistance reaches, say, 3 MPa.

soil-phys-158.q: Why can't the expansion of freezing water explain frost heave?
soil-phys-158.a: Water expands only about 9%, too little; by 1930 Stephen Taber had shown that water migrates to the freeze line, and that benzene, which contracts on freezing, also heaves.

soil-phys-185.q: How does wetting change a soil's thermal conductivity?
soil-phys-185.a: It raises it: dry soil conducts about 0.2–0.4 W·m−1·K−1 and wet soil 1–3, and varying moisture largely determines a soil's conductivity because air conducts heat poorly.

soil-chem-198.q: How do soil minerals retain phosphorus in acid and in calcareous soils?
soil-chem-198.a: In acid soils by adsorption onto iron and aluminium oxyhydroxides; in neutral to calcareous soils by precipitation onto calcite.

soil-chem-108.a: Water is not adsorbed between its layers; its CEC is low as well.

soil-chem-161.q: Which iron(III) oxyhydroxides matter most in soils?
soil-chem-161.a: Goethite and lepidocrocite, the commonest forms and the most important mineral carriers of iron in soils.

soil-chem-103.q: Rank AlCl3, CaCl2 and NaCl by how well they flocculate colloids.
soil-chem-103.a: AlCl3 > CaCl2 > NaCl, because multivalent cations flocculate colloids more efficiently than monovalent ones.

soil-chem-203.q: What does the Langmuir isotherm predict at low and high pressure?
soil-chem-203.a: θ = Kp/(1 + Kp), the fraction of sites occupied, is about Kp at low pressure and approaches 1 at high pressure.

soil-chem-174.q: Below what redox potential do methanogens grow, and to which domain do they belong?
soil-chem-174.a: Below −0.3 V; all known methanogens belong to the domain Archaea.

soil-chem-028.q: Why did land clearing bring salt to the surface in Australia?
soil-chem-028.a: Deep-rooted native vegetation had used groundwater year-round; once crops and pasture replaced it, rising groundwater brought stored salt up, and evaporation left it in the soil.

soil-chem-025.q: How do seeps differ from scalds?
soil-chem-025.a: Both are saline discharge areas: seeps are where groundwater meets the soil surface, scalds where water is lost by evaporation only.

soil-bio-067.q: What do Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter each oxidize?
soil-bio-067.a: Nitrosomonas oxidizes ammonia to nitrite, and Nitrobacter oxidizes nitrite to nitrate.

soil-bio-065.q: Why are earthworm casts taken as a sign of healthy soil?
soil-bio-065.a: Casts often hold more plant-available nutrients than the surrounding soil and build stable soil aggregates, marking biologically active soil.

soil-bio-030.q: Which energy channels did soil flow webs reveal?
soil-bio-030.a: The bacterial and fungal channels, which carry the largest flow, and the root-herbivory channel, which carries much less.

soil-bio-208.q: Why do the pines of the pygmy forest stay so small?
soil-bio-208.a: Their podzol, the Blacklock series, is very acid, nutrient-poor and high in exchangeable aluminium, and its iron hardpan blocks deep roots and internal drainage.

soil-bio-151.q: How do mycorrhizal hyphae reach soil that roots cannot?
soil-bio-151.a: Most are far finer than the smallest root or root hair, so they explore soil that roots cannot reach and add absorbing surface.

soil-bio-163.q: Why do orchid seedlings depend on a fungus?
soil-bio-163.a: Orchid seeds, 0.35–1.50 mm long, carry virtually no energy reserve, so seedlings get their carbon from the fungus.

soil-bio-153.q: How much nitrogen do grain legumes fix each year?
soil-bio-153.a: Grown on about 1.5 million km2 a year, they fix about 44–66 million tons, almost half of the nitrogen used in agriculture.

soil-bio-111.q: How do detritivores and microbes break detritus down together?
soil-bio-111.a: Detritivores digest mainly the protein-rich microbes and excrete the detritus barely changed; microbes regrow on that dung and it is eaten again, until the detritus is fragmented and its complex carbohydrates disappear.

soil-bio-101.q: How much of the carbon in soil can microbial necromass make up?
soil-bio-101.a: 30 to 80%, because microbes cycle soil carbon so extensively.

soil-bio-270.q: What does a Q10 of 2 to 3 mean for a biological rate?
soil-bio-270.a: The rate doubles or triples with every 10 °C, as in most biological systems.

soil-class-017.q: What organic carbon content separates mineral from organic material?
soil-class-017.a: Mineral material has less than 20% soil organic carbon; organic material has 20% or more.

soil-class-106.q: What base saturation separates Alfisols from Ultisols?
soil-class-106.a: Alfisols have at least 35% base saturation; the more leached Ultisols fall below 35%.

soil-class-120.q: In the WRB, what decides whether redox features make a Gleysol or a Stagnosol?
soil-class-120.a: Features from rising groundwater make a Gleysol; those from stagnant surface water make a Stagnosol or Planosol.

soil-class-146.a: Repeated wetting and drying: plinthite, a red clay-rich material sometimes over 80% iron oxides, then hardens irreversibly.

soil-fert-184.q: Why does residue with a C:N above 30:1 lower the nitrogen available to plants?
soil-fert-184.a: Microbes are left short of nitrogen, so they take up soil ammonium and nitrate and immobilize them; below 15, mineral nitrogen is freed for plants.

soil-fert-231.q: Why do older leaves yellow first when nitrogen runs short?
soil-fert-231.a: The plant moves nitrogen out of them to younger tissue.

soil-fert-227.q: Why does calcium deficiency show first in new, fast-growing parts?
soil-fert-227.a: Calcium does not move in the phloem, so low-transpiring tissues and new, fast-growing parts suffer first.

soil-fert-137.q: Why does potassium leach from plants faster than nitrogen or phosphorus?
soil-fert-137.a: It exists only as the small soluble K+ ion.

soil-fert-079.q: Why may marled crops show magnesium deficiency?
soil-fert-079.a: Marl's carbonate is mostly calcium carbonate, so magnesium must be supplied as well.

soil-fert-026.q: How much nitrogen does a green manure release?
soil-fert-026.a: Depending on the species, 45 to 224 kg/ha (40 to 200 lb/acre), and usually 40-60% of the crop's nitrogen becomes available to the next crop.

soil-fert-057.q: Why must agricultural lime be finely ground?
soil-fert-057.a: Soil acids are weak: particles over 8 mesh are of little value, 8–60 mesh somewhat effective, and finer than 60 mesh fully effective.

soil-fert-207.q: How much phosphogypsum does making phosphoric acid leave behind?
soil-fert-207.a: Five tons for each ton of phosphoric acid, an impure radioactive waste; 100 to 280 million tons are produced yearly.

soil-water-091.q: When does saturation-excess overland flow begin, unlike Hortonian flow?
soil-water-091.a: Only once the soil itself is saturated; Hortonian flow is also called unsaturated overland flow.

soil-water-014.q: Why do clay-rich soils resist erosion better than sandy or silty ones?

soil-water-055.q: What safety factor makes a slope stable, and which values call for monitoring?
soil-water-055.a: A slope is globally stable if the safety factor exceeds 1 along every potential sliding surface; values between about 1 and 1.3 mark marginally stable slopes that need monitoring or stabilization.

soil-water-030.q: How high does wind usually lift sand?
soil-water-030.a: Most stays within 50 cm of the surface, and practically none rises above 2 m.

soil-water-106.q: How much can active pore water pressure cut a soil's shear strength?
soil-water-106.a: By up to 60%, because rising water content weakens shear strength and so cohesion.

soil-water-269.q: What does the Shields number compare?
soil-water-269.a: It is proportional to the ratio of the fluid force on a particle to the particle's weight.

soil-water-146.q: Why does a rich fen keep a fairly stable pH?
soil-water-146.a: Groundwater passing limestone dissolves some calcium carbonate, and the bicarbonate produced buffers the fen's pH.

soil-phys-162.q: In Penck's slope replacement, where does flattening begin?
soil-phys-162.a: At the lowest slope, spreading upward and backward: flattening always occurs from the bottom up.

soil-agri-006.q: Why is crop rotation not a form of intercropping?
soil-agri-006.a: Its crops grow in separate seasons.

soil-agri-057.q: Why does filling planting pits with manure and compost raise yields so much?
soil-agri-057.a: The organic matter attracts termites whose tunnels break up the soil; yields of trees, sorghum and millet can rise by up to 500 percent.

soil-agri-098.q: How much can no-till cut nitrous oxide emissions?
soil-agri-098.a: By 40–70% depending on rotation, which matters because nitrous oxide is 300 times stronger than CO2 and lasts 120 years.

soil-agri-112.q: How deep does a subsoiler work compared with most tillage tools?
soil-agri-112.a: Most tools work the top 15–20 cm (6–8 in); a subsoiler loosens soil to twice that depth, usually 45–75 cm (18–30 in) or more.

soil-agri-158.q: How do buffer strips protect surface waters?
soil-agri-158.a: By slowing surface runoff, they trap sediment and filter out nutrients and pesticides before these reach the water.

soil-agri-083.q: How does a digital terrain model differ from a digital surface model?
soil-agri-083.a: A digital terrain model shows the bare ground surface, while a digital surface model may include tree canopy and buildings.

soil-meth-019.q: How does the Kjeldahl method measure nitrogen?
soil-meth-019.a: Concentrated sulfuric acid at 360–410 °C digests the sample and holds its nitrogen as ammonium sulfate; sodium hydroxide turns this into ammonia gas, which is distilled into a standard acid and measured by titration.

soil-meth-012.q: Why can soil moisture shift the NDVI without any change in vegetation?
soil-meth-012.a: Wet soil darkens, and bare soils themselves give small positive values of about 0.1 to 0.2.

soil-env-273.q: How much CO2 does silicate weathering sequester per mole of calcium or magnesium released?
soil-env-273.a: In theory 1 mol of CO2 for each mol of Ca2+ or Mg2+, though natural ratios vary with temperature and CO2 pressure.

soil-env-070.q: How much land do drylands cover, and how many people live there?
soil-env-070.a: 41.3% of Earth's land surface, home to more than 2 billion people.

soil-env-091.q: Why did soils improve under agrivoltaic systems in the Kubuqi Desert?
soil-env-091.a: Panel shade cut soil temperature and evaporation, and the panels acted as windbreaks that stopped sand burying plants, creating a better microclimate with the vegetation.

soil-env-097.q: What removal rates do bioretention systems typically achieve?
soil-env-097.a: About 80% of suspended solids and 50–60% of heavy metals; a 2025 meta-analysis found nitrogen and phosphorus loads cut by about 55% and 62%.

soil-env-002.q: How long does DDT persist in soil?
soil-env-002.a: Its half-life in soil is 2–15 years, so residues are still found in people, though at levels 5 to 10 times lower than in the 1970s.

soil-env-031.q: Why can heavy metal pollutants never biodegrade?
soil-env-031.a: Almost all compounds biodegrade given time, but elements do not.

soil-env-013.q: Which fuels does air sparging suit, and which does it not?
soil-env-013.a: It suits light gasoline constituents such as benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylene, but not heavier fuels such as kerosene and diesel.

soil-env-221.q: Why are LNAPLs easier to locate and remove than DNAPLs?
soil-env-221.a: An LNAPL is buoyant, so it stops at the water table and floats on it.

soil-env-266.q: How much caesium did mustard greens remove in the Chernobyl zone?
soil-env-266.a: Up to 22% of average caesium activity in one growing season.

soil-env-299.q: What most likely drives parrots on the Manu River to eat soil?
soil-env-299.a: Sodium: consumed soils are consistently higher in it, and geophagy increases with distance from the ocean.

soil-hist-129.q: How does lead-210 reveal soil erosion?
soil-hist-129.a: Excess lead-210 from fallout builds up in surface soils, and its activity profile with depth reconstructs soil redistribution over the past century, giving erosion and deposition rates.

soil-hist-091.q: How do a buried wall and a buried ditch show up as cropmarks?
soil-hist-091.a: A buried wall diverts water and displaces fertile soil, stunting crops, while an organic-rich ditch fill holds water and boosts growth.

soil-hist-115.q: Why did grain output on the Kazakh steppe fall after early success?
soil-hist-115.a: Only 200 to 350 mm of rain fell a year, the soils were salty, winds caused erosion in spring, and grain monoculture, on 83% of cropland in 1958–1959, depleted nutrients.

soil-hist-108.q: Where did Lawes and Gilbert find that cereals get their nitrogen?
soil-hist-108.a: From the soil, contrary to Liebig's view that it came only from the air.

soil-hist-078.q: Since when has the Soil Science Society of America's flagship journal appeared only online?
soil-hist-078.a: Since 2013, with double-blind review of its articles.
